summary:
Planet X and SPHEREx es una herramienta web gratuita que utiliza los datos infrarrojos de la misión SPHEREx de la NASA para explorar cambios en el cielo a lo largo del tiempo. Permite a estudiantes, investigadores y científicos ciudadanos detectar asteroides, cometas, enanas marrones y estrellas variables sin necesidad de programar ni instalar software.
Su funcionamiento se basa en ingresar coordenadas celestes para obtener, alinear y animar imágenes desde la base de datos de la NASA (IRSA). Entre sus funciones principales destacan los modos de comparación de imágenes, la superposición de catálogos astronómicos (Gaia DR3 y AllWISE) y el cálculo instantáneo de espectros y curvas de luz, cuyos datos pueden exportarse en formato CSV y compartirse mediante un enlace.
La plataforma fue validada con éxito utilizando objetivos reales como la estrella de Barnard. Además, su arquitectura web optimiza el peso de los archivos astronómicos para garantizar una carga rápida y accesible desde cualquier dispositivo.
details:
Planet X and SPHEREx is a free web tool for watching NASA's SPHEREx infrared sky survey change over time. You enter a right ascension and declination, or tap one of six example targets. The tool finds every SPHEREx snapshot covering that spot and plays them as a short film, so anything that moves stands out. Distant stars stay put, while brown dwarfs, nearby stars, asteroids and comets drift. Variable stars pulse.

How it works.

  • A small server queries NASA/IPAC IRSA for the snapshots that cover the spot and downloads small cutouts of each one.
  • It lines the cutouts up on one common sky grid.
  • The browser plays them back.

Features.

  • Combine and compare: play every snapshot, one sum per infrared colour band (D1–D6), or one sum per observing visit. You can also subtract the typical sky to make movers show as a bright and dark pair.
  • Follow a mover: a co-moving mode holds a known mover still while the stars trail.
  • Overlays and size: Gaia DR3 and AllWISE overlays, and a field of view from 1′ to 20′.
  • Measure: click any spot to get its spectrum (brightness against wavelength) and its light curve (brightness over time), with CSV export. Each snapshot also shows its quality flags.
  • Sharing: the whole state lives in the URL, so views can be shared or embedded.

Benefits and impact. SPHEREx produces far more data than any one person can inspect. The tool lets anyone, with no software or coding, take part in the kind of discovery behind Pluto and Backyard Worlds. It is aimed at citizen scientists, students and educators. It also gives researchers a quick way to look at a source across all six detector bands and across dates.

Testing. We checked it on all six featured targets: Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae and R Draconis. For WISE 0855, Barnard's Star and Epsilon Indi, real detections landed within a few arcseconds of their predicted positions. RW Aurigae and R Draconis loaded and measured correctly, and R Draconis showed clear brightness changes.

Built with.

  • Astro and TypeScript, with Canvas for rendering and no charting library.
  • Hand-written FITS parsing and WCS reprojection (TAN projection with SIP distortion).
  • IRSA SIA cutouts, Gaia and AllWISE queries, CDS Sesame for name lookup, and deployment on Vercel.

What's creative. We built a three-step guided interface (pick a spot, watch it change, dig deeper) with plain language and examples that say what to look for. Spectra and light curves are computed on the fly from the same click. New data releases are added by editing one line of configuration.

What we considered.

  • Data volume: every SPHEREx cutout carries about 4 MB of unused PSF data, so a server downloads it and sends the browser only about 100 kB per frame, with caching.
  • Pixel flags: we worked out the flag bits ourselves, because the public docs don't tabulate them. We found that masking saturation flags would erase real star cores.
  • Accessibility: the page works on phones, with keyboard control and support for reduced motion.
